items.title: Pre-Deployment Cardiovascular Risk Assessment and Outcomes among United States Antarctic Program Participants: Insights from Contemporary Risk Models
items.summary: Background: Cardiovascular (CV) screening is critical for personnel deploying to Antarctica, where geographic isolation and limited medical care make the management of acute cardiovascular events challenging. The utility of contemporary risk prediction tools such as the AHA PREVENT equations in this unique population remains uncertain. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 154 individuals referred for enhanced CV evaluation before deployment to the U.S. Antarctic Program (USAP). Participants were evaluated across three temporal cohorts (2018-2020, 2021-2023, and 2024-2026). Demographics, CV risk factors, cardiac testing, and deployment clearance outcomes were collected. Risk was estimated using the Framingham Risk Score (FRS), AHA/ACC Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE), and AHA PREVENT risk models. Results: The cohort was predominantly male (79.9%; mean age 44.6 {+/-} 14.6 years), and abnormal ECG was the most common referral trigger (70.8%). Median 10-year risk was low by PREVENT and FRS and borderline elevated by PCE (PREVENT 2.7% [IQR 1.1-6.6], FRS 2.3% [IQR 0.5-7.1], and PCE 6.1% [IQR 2.4-9.2]). Among 72 participants with all scores, 51% were classified discordantly; PREVENT ASCVD agreed closely with FRS (=0.77) but poorly with PCE (=0.24-0.35), which consistently estimated higher risk. PCE was calculable in 52.6% versus 70.8% for PREVENT. Overall, 132 participants (85.7%) were cleared for deployment, while 8 (5.2%) were not physically qualified (NPQ); 6 of these NPQs were due to cardiovascular causes. Of 22 cardiac medical evacuations during the study period, 21 involved individuals without prior advanced cardiovascular screening. One screened individual was evacuated for symptoms subsequently found to have no cardiac cause. Conclusions: Risk calculators disagree substantially in the fitness-selected population. items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6534: Detection and Classification of Physiological Activation States Through Biosignal Analysis Using Machine Learning
items.summary: Monitoring autonomic nervous system responses offers significant potential for personalized health applications and early intervention. This study presents a machine learning framework for binary classification of physiological activation states using electrocardiogram (ECG) and respiratory (RESP) signals from the WESAD dataset. Stress and amusement were grouped as Activation, whereas baseline and meditation were grouped as Non-Activation. The processing pipeline incorporates R-peak detection, temporal segmentation, handcrafted feature extraction, and subject-independent evaluation. Conventional machine learning classifiers and deep learning architectures were evaluated, together with a proposed Hybrid Multi-Scale Temporal Convolutional-Conformer (MST-Conformer) combining temporal representations learned from ECG and RESP waveforms with handcrafted physiological features. Performance was assessed using 15-fold Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validation. Adding respiration-derived features to ECG-derived features improved conventional machine learning performance, increasing the highest balanced accuracy from 0.752 to 0.807 and AUC from 0.802 to 0.886. The complete Hybrid MST-Conformer incorporating 27 physiological features achieved a mean accuracy of 0.825, balanced accuracy of 0.820, F1-score of 0.763, and AUC of 0.904. Subject-level analysis also revealed substantial physiological heterogeneity. These results support the potential of combining learned temporal representations with handcrafted physiological information for subject-independent physiological activation classification.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6511: Development of a Wearable Torsion Sensor Utilizing a Geometric Model and a Hysteresis-Compensated Calibration Engine
items.summary: Measuring torsional movement is crucial for tracking human kinematics in applications such as virtual reality, biomechanics, rehabilitation, and soft robotic joints. However, continuous, non-invasive torsion measurement remains challenging due to multi-axial deformations, where existing methods rely heavily on empirical data fitting or computationally expensive deep learning models requiring vast training datasets. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a training-free, highly precise torsion estimation framework that converts soft resistive strain sensor data into forearm rotation angles using closed-form kinematic-geometric modeling. Two geometric representations-the Cylinder Model and Truncated Cone Model-are established to analytically map non-linear tensile strain to torsion angles. Additionally, an online calibration algorithm is integrated to mitigate cumulative measurement drift caused by viscoelastic hysteresis. Under static conditions, the proposed models achieved a high coefficient of determination (R2 = 0.9888) against reference IMU data. In dynamic trials, the hysteresis compensation algorithm maintained robust tracking performance (R2 = 0.8033), achieving an angular root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 4.12° and a cycle peak prominence relative error of 0.42% for the Truncated Cone Model. In this single-subject proof-of-concept feasibility study (n = 1), the proposed framework demonstrated the feasibility of continuous torsional motion tracking through a training-free geometric approach, providing a preliminary foundation for future evaluation in wearable systems and soft robotics.

items.title: The autonomic-ventricular coherence index: a novel single-lead ECG method with acquisition-dependent discrimination

Coherence was integrated over the high-frequency band (0.15–0.40 Hz). items.title: GlucoSense: early diabetes risk assessment via fusion of human activity recognition and glucose prediction
items.summary: Non-Insulin-Dependent Diabetes Mellitus (NIDDM) is a chronic and progressive metabolic disease characterized by chronically high blood glucose levels. It is a disease with an often asymptomatic onset, which means that a high percentage of affected individuals remain unidentified until quite far in the disease process, thereby underlining the importance of a good, reliable screening instrument for proactive detection. In this paper, GlucoSense is introduced as a single framework for early NIDDM risk stratification by combining Human Activity Recognition (HAR) with continuous blood glucose forecasting using two Graph Attention Network version 2 (GATv2)-based architectures. The first is a HAR module trained with smartphone triaxial accelerometer data that covers 23 activity classes, while the second is a glucose prediction module trained with the OhioT1DM dataset to predict glucose levels for a 30 min horizon. Unlike sequential models, GlucoSense encodes complex dependencies between movement patterns, cardiac activity, nutrition, and glycemic behaviour by modeling relationships in a graph structure. The study was longitudinal, spanning 90 days, with six participants. Three important clinical parameters, mean glucose level, time above hyperglycemic level, and glycemic coefficient of variance were calculated. The system was able to correctly identify metabolically healthy individuals and those with prediabetic patterns. The framework was cross-validated with HbA1c laboratory tests to verify the clinical consistency of the framework. Both modules were benchmarked against sequential, convolutional, attention-based, and graph-based baselines under an identical protocol with five independent runs. The glucose module lowered the root mean squared error from 31.82 mg/dL for an LSTM baseline to 25.60 mg/dL, and the activity module reached 98.50% accuracy, with every difference confirmed by paired significance testing and reported with 95% confidence intervals. items.title: Contactless gait-derived features as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity in adolescents
items.summary: Timely assessment of depression severity in adolescents is essential for guiding clinical care, yet conventional evaluations rely on episodic clinical assessments and symptom rating scales. Contactless gait analysis offers a potentially scalable approach to capturing objective behavioral features associated with depression. Here, we introduce the Long-Distance 3D Adolescent Depression Gait Dataset (LD3D-ADG), comprising depth-sensor gait recordings from 119 adolescents at a single center, including 39 healthy controls, 41 with mild depression, and 39 with moderate-to-severe depression. We developed UMLPA-GCN, a graph convolutional network that models spatiotemporal gait dynamics across three anatomically defined skeletal partitions. In participant-independent five-fold cross-validation, UMLPA-GCN achieved 75.63% classification accuracy, a macro-F1 score of 75.52%, and a macro-area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.839 (95% confidence interval, 0.779--0.899). Class-specific recall was 87.18%, 63.41%, and 76.92% for healthy controls, mild depression, and moderate-to-severe depression, respectively. At the participant level, reduced arm swing, slower pelvic movement, restricted joint range of motion, and greater arm-swing asymmetry were identified as leading potential digital biomarkers contributing to depression severity assessment, associated with higher 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence for contactless digital depression severity stratification in adolescents. Further external and prospective validation is needed to establish their utility for longitudinal monitoring and timely clinical assessment.

items.title: Task-evoked eye movements as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults
items.summary: Objective digital measures of depression severity could complement conventional symptom assessments and facilitate more timely clinical evaluation. Here, we investigated whether task-evoked eye movements provide interpretable behavioral markers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults. In this single-center, cross-sectional study, 155 participants aged 14--20 years completed emotional-spatial free-viewing and memory-guided recall tasks and were stratified by 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. We examined 19 prespecified eye-movement features across six task-informed domains using covariate-adjusted ordinal-trend models. Greater depression severity was associated with lower gaze-allocation entropy (standardized $β=-0.599$), fewer inter-area switches ($β=-0.526$), longer first target-entry latency ($β=0.572$), and lower target dwell proportion ($β=-0.678$; all false-discovery-rate-adjusted $q<0.001$). Emotion-specific attentional-bias measures were not associated with severity, whereas associations involving fixation dispersion weakened after adjustment for anxiety symptoms. In a complementary machine-learning analysis incorporating 44 candidate eye-movement features and demographic covariates, a three-stage cascade classifier achieved the highest four-class stratification performance (accuracy, 0.665; macro-F1, 0.670; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.869), outperforming single-stage and two-stage approaches. Together, these findings identify altered visual exploration and memory-guided gaze control as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity, rather than generalized negative attentional bias. These results support further prospective evaluation of task-evoked eye tracking as a complementary approach for timely severity assessment and clinical decision support.

items.title: FALLNEST: Dual-Domain Dataset Condensation of Imbalanced IMU Data for Wearable Fall Detection
items.summary: Wearable fall detection is hampered by rare fall events, scarce labeled IMU data, and the cost of training deep models on large, imbalanced corpora. Existing methods either rely on hand-crafted features with shallow classifiers, which limits learning from raw signals, or train deep networks on full datasets that require re-sampling to counter class skew and demand substantial data and compute. To address this, we propose a novel Fall detection framework via Normalized-gradient and Embedding matched Synthetic Time-frequency condensation, dubbed FALLNEST, a data-centric approach that distills large, imbalanced IMU datasets into tiny, class-balanced synthetic training sets. Building on dual-domain time-series condensation (CondTSC), FALLNEST introduces a fall-specific 7-channel input with accelerometer vector magnitude, class-balanced K-Means initialization, and normalized gradient matching with gradient clipping, combined with MMD-based embedding alignment and multi-view Fourier-domain augmentation, so that class balance arises from the condensed set itself rather than from re-sampling. We evaluate on SisFall, KFall, and MobiFall using strict subject-wise splits and naturally imbalanced test sets, reporting accuracy, Macro-F1, and PR-AUC over five seeds. A 102K-parameter TinyCNN trained on only 32 to 146 synthetic windows (about only 1% of the training windows) reaches 93.5-95.8% mean accuracy and 0.89-0.98 PR-AUC, with standard deviations of 1.0-1.7% in accuracy, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach.

items.title: ECG-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Targeted Electrocardiogram Waveform Evolution
items.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need supervision that targets evolving weaknesses and remains faithful to waveform evidence. We introduce ECG-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework combining verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search. Signal remeasurement verifies waveform edits; construction errors guide generator repair, while learner errors motivate interventions compared on a separate selection set. Across seven benchmarks, three rounds raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean question-answering accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04% and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. Across the retained trajectory, the preferred supervision shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts. Continued feedback correction yields diminishing external gains. These results motivate separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and checking whether gains on the feedback set transfer to independent benchmarks.

items.title: A Co-Located MMG-FES Wearable Interface for Action-Updated State-Gated Stimulation
items.summary: Functional electrical stimulation (FES) assists movement, but fixed schedules cannot track how a repeatedly activated muscle changes, and surface electromyography (EMG) near the stimulation electrodes is often obscured by artifacts. Prior work recorded mechanomyography (MMG) passively during closed-loop FES cycling and estimated FES-induced fatigue or predicted fatigue for FES control, without gating stimulation with stimulated-site MMG. In this study, we present VG-FES, a wearable module co-locating microphone-based MMG, programmable charge-balanced biphasic stimulation, and embedded state-gated control at one on-skin thigh site. After each action, we compare rectus femoris (RF) mean power frequency (MPF) with an early-session baseline of the same direction, giving a relative state. A threshold on its window means enables fixed-duration bursts separated by rest periods. During onboard stimulation, MMG remained recordable, whereas near-site EMG was artifact-dominated. Under prolonged external stimulation, cycle-wise MMG tracked an independent local-pressure reference (Spearman rho = 0.968). In leave-one-session-out evaluation on 2284 squat actions (11 sessions, eight participants), MMG-based action segmentation reached an event-detection F1 of 0.923 and direction classification a balanced accuracy of 0.925. Online, over 15.69 min of self-paced squats, one participant received four bursts while MMG acquisition and action monitoring continued. Mechanical feedback from the stimulated site offers wearable FES and assistive robotics a per-action basis for state-gated stimulation.

items.title: Integration of Ecological Momentary Assessment and Intervention With Wearable-Based Digital Phenotypes to Treat Anxiety in Young Adults: Mixed Methods Experimental Study
items.summary: Background: Young adults report high levels of anxiety, yet their access to timely treatment remains limited. Mobile-based digital therapeutics, particularly ecological momentary assessment and intervention (EMA/EMI), offer a promising approach to deliver context-responsive care. The integration of wearable-derived digital phenotypes with digital therapeutics may enhance the personalization of feedback in such interventions, but empirical evidence from real-world settings remains scarce. Objective: This study examined the real-world applicability and effectiveness of an EMA/EMI-based digital therapeutic, ANZEILAX-Green (HAII Corp), for use in anxiety reduction in young adults and investigated how personalized feedback generated by combining EMA/EMI data with wearable-based digital phenotypes ameliorates symptoms and promotes self-management and user engagement. Methods: An 8-week exploratory experimental study was conducted with young adults aged 19-39 years. Participants used a smartphone app in which EMA/EMI modules had been integrated with a smartwatch that continuously collected digital phenotyping data, including heart rate, sleep, and activity. Quantitative changes were analyzed using paired-samples t tests and repeated-measures ANOVA, and qualitative interviews were thematically analyzed to identify user experience mechanisms and design implications. items.title: Diagnostic performance of the ECG-SMART AI score for detecting angiographically significant coronary artery disease in patients undergoing elective coronary angiography
items.summary: by Dania A. Bani Hani, Jafar A. Alshraideh, Hamza Alduraidi, Akram Saleh, Nathan T. Riek, Karam Daoud, Rui Qi Ji, Samir Saba, Clifton W. We previously developed an artificial intelligence–enhanced ECG (AI-ECG) model for detecting acute coronary occlusion. items.title: AI-Driven Urge Regulation Assistant (AURA): Designing Preemptive Smart Wearables for Smoking Cessation
items.summary: Smoking cessation remains a complex self-regulatory challenge, often undermined by cue-triggered cravings arising from habitual, emotional, and social contexts. Existing wearable cessation systems are largely reactive, detecting smoking events only after lapses occur and thus missing the critical window for timely intervention. Guided by cue-reactivity theory and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), we argue that future digital health systems should shift from retrospective feedback toward proactive craving management that supports user autonomy and competence. To inform the design of such systems, we present a formative pilot qualitative study involving semi-structured interviews with 10 smokers and ex-smokers from a multi-ethnic Asian population, a demographic underrepresented in current wearable AI and smoking cessation research. Through an iterative co-design interview process, we examine (1) the barriers and facilitators to smoking cessation and (2) the desired design features of wearable systems targeting cravings before lapses occur. Our findings identify key craving predictors across habitual, emotional, and social dimensions, alongside user-preferred intervention strategies such as social accountability, personalized support, rewards, and just-in-time distraction techniques. Participants also emphasized the importance of trust, privacy, personalization, and non-judgmental interaction styles. These insights directly inform the design of AURA, a novel smartwatch-smartphone ecosystem for proactive craving detection and intervention using commercially available wearable devices.

items.title: BeatFlow-ECG: Rectified Flow for ECG Reconstruction from Indirect Wearable Signals
items.summary: Continuous cardiac monitoring outside clinical settings requires signals that are both informative and practical to collect during daily life. Electrocardiography (ECG) provides rich information about cardiac rhythm and waveform morphology, while wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) is easier to acquire continuously but is only an indirect cardiovascular measurement and is highly sensitive to motion. We present BeatFlow-ECG, a conditional rectified-flow model for reconstructing single-channel ECG from synchronized PPG and inertial measurements. BeatFlow-ECG models reconstruction as conditional transport from noise to ECG using a convolutional encoder-decoder with a transformer bottleneck and explicit flow-time conditioning. Motion information is incorporated through IMU-derived conditioning features, motion-dependent loss weighting, and an easy-to-hard training curriculum. We evaluate the model under leave-one-subject-out protocols on PPG-DaLiA and WESAD. BeatFlow-ECG achieves the best results among the evaluated deterministic, adversarial, and diffusion-based baselines across all reported waveform and beat-timing metrics, with Pearson correlations of 0.983 and 0.986 and R-peak F1 scores of 0.946 and 0.955, respectively. Compared with Conditional DDPM-1D, L1 error decreases from 0.085 to 0.062 on PPG-DaLiA and from 0.074 to 0.055 on WESAD. Additional analyses on PPG-DaLiA show higher correlation in fixed R-peak-relative waveform regions and lower reconstruction error across low-, medium-, and high-motion subsets.

items.title: REFIT: Recognize, Fix, and Test Wearable Sensor Placement Shifts without Labels
items.summary: We present REFIT, an input calibration for frozen activity-recognition models whose inertial sensors are worn differently at deployment than in training. When users move a watch to the other wrist or put a strap sensor back on turned, the model sees the same motion on changed axes. REFIT undoes such shifts without labels or retraining. It describes them by families of axis transforms, such as reflections and rotations, and fits each family to the user's data so that simple statistics match those of the training data. The family that removes most of the mismatch names the shift. REFIT fixes the shift by applying the best member of that family before the frozen model and re-estimating its normalization statistics. It tests the fixed model with a label-free accuracy estimate and asks the user to re-wear the sensor when it is low. Experiments on real left/right sensor pairs and on real and simulated re-attachment show that REFIT outperforms label-free test-time adaptation methods on every dataset and restores most of the accuracy lost to re-attachment. It names injected shifts far more reliably than a confidence-based selector. After a correction over all signed permutations of the axes, the estimate separates successful from failed corrections.

items.title: Label-Efficient Deep Learning for ECG Delineation: A Multi-Dataset Benchmark against Widely Used Delineation Tools
items.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) delineation, the identification of waveform boundaries, is a foundational step that translates raw ECG signals into clinically interpretable measurements. Deep learning has advanced this task but remains dependent on costly expert annotations. Label-efficient strategies such as self-supervised pretraining and semi-supervised learning are expected to ease this burden, yet it remains unclear whether they yield reliable delineation and whether the deep models they produce outperform the delineation tools used in practice. We address this in two stages. First, comparing self-supervised objectives with supervised or semi-supervised fine-tuning across one internal and four external datasets, we find that pretraining helps but the objective matters, and that the value of semi-supervised fine-tuning depends on the pretraining objective. Second, we benchmark the selected deep learning model against widely used open-source (NeuroKit2, Prominence, ECGdeli) and commercial (CalECG) tools using three complementary metrics. The model ranks best on every metric and dataset, outperforming the strongest tool by a clear margin on the rhythm-diverse set (mIoU 71.3 vs. 54.8%; averaged point-wise sensitivity 92.6 vs. 76.4%), and degrades the least from sinus to arrhythmia. A rhythm-stratified and point-wise analysis further characterizes the distinctive behavior of each tool, yielding practical guidance for tool selection. These results provide systematic, multi-dataset evidence that self-supervised pretraining is effective for ECG delineation and enables a label-efficiently trained deep learning model to outperform widely used delineation tools by leveraging abundant unlabeled data. This supports adopting such models in diverse, real-world clinical settings.

items.title: Characterizing the Performance Gap in Human Activity Recognition for Older Adults
items.summary: Human activity recognition (HAR) from wrist-worn accelerometers is increasingly used for health and behavioral tracking. Yet, most wearable HAR models are developed and evaluated on datasets dominated by younger adults, leaving it unclear whether benchmark progress generalizes across age groups. In this work, we leverage MyMove, our carefully annotated, free-living older-adult HAR dataset (mean age 71), to evaluate deep-learning architectures and training regimes under both leave-one-subject-out and cross-dataset transfer. We find that improvements on younger-adult benchmarks fail to transfer equally to data collected from older adults, resulting in a persistent and often widening performance gap. However, richer representations, particularly frozen self-supervised features pretrained on the age-diverse UK Biobank dataset, substantially improve performance on data from older adults and consistently narrow the performance gap, at modest cost to younger-adult performance, though disparities remain. These findings suggest that benchmark gains and architectural scaling alone provide an incomplete picture of progress in wearable HAR, and broader advances may require representations that better capture population diversity, alongside personalized adaptation to individual movement patterns and routines.

items.title: Open-Source Multi-Wire SPI Readout for Wearable Ultrasound Probes
items.summary: Wearable ultrasound probes must transfer increasingly large acquisition payloads while maintaining compact, low-power electronics. In TinyProbe, the current bottleneck in data transfer occurs between the acquisition FPGA and the wireless system controller. This work presents an open-source, multi-wire SPI readout interface that uses serial command and address phases followed by a build-time-selectable dual- or quad-lane payload phase that is intended to address this bottleneck by increasing the potential bandwidth over the wifi limit while retaining compatibility with the Microcontroller-centric wearable US architecture. The interface emulates a serial flash memory, enabling compatibility with a broad range of microcontroller families and their existing peripheral interfaces. On the FPGA, the data path connects the existing acquisition FIFOs to the SPI interface through clock-domain crossing, sample reshaping, and packing into 32-bit words. Dual-SPI readout is integrated into the existing IGLOO2/SiWG917 TinyProbe architecture and verified at an SCLK frequency of 5 MHz. A separate Kria K26 testbed is used to characterize the FPGA SPI interface independently of the acquisition and wireless subsystems, demonstrating error-free transfers at SCLK frequencies up to 66 MHz. These measurements identify the SiWG917 multi-lane SPI implementation as the next bandwidth-limiting component and motivate a future upgrade of the system controller. The HDL and MCU implementations are released under a permissive open-source license.

items.title: ECG-Scroll: A Long-Horizon, Streaming Benchmark and Agent Environment for Interpretation of Ambulatory Electrocardiograms
items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can now interpret a standard ten-second, twelve-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) with clinically grounded, reward-verified reasoning. Real cardiac monitoring is different. Ambulatory (Holter) and telemetry recordings span hours to days and are read as they stream in, and their clinically decisive findings are paroxysmal, brief episodes buried in an otherwise unremarkable trace. Such a recording cannot be held in one context at diagnostic resolution, and its future has not yet happened, so a reader must work online, deciding what to measure now, committing evidence to memory as it passes, and reporting events as they occur. We recast long-duration ECG interpretation as a long-horizon, online (streaming, causal) sequential decision process and introduce ECG-Scroll. As a benchmark, long ambulatory recordings are streamed to an agent chunk by chunk, and it must localize, quantify, and promptly flag paroxysmal events without access to future signal; because the underlying signal is retained, every answer is checkable against objective ground truth, giving rule-based rather than judge-based rewards, and the streaming formulation adds a metric batch evaluation cannot express, the detection latency between an event's onset and the moment the agent records it. As an agent environment, it is a fixed, gym-style interaction layer that exercises three competencies single-glance ECG models never touch: Memory, Tool use through signal-grounded measurement rather than reading pixels, and Planning of what to measure now and when to commit. We release 390 whole-recording instances spanning 2,536 hours of two-lead ambulatory ECG and evaluate a signal-threshold rule agent alongside off-the-shelf LLM agents online, characterizing how they use memory, tools, and planning and where the benchmark's head-room lies.

items.title: Skill Profiling with Attributable Reasoning (SPAR): A Wearable Analysis System for Boxing
items.summary: A punch is a ballistic, full-body action driven by a kinetic chain running from the legs through the trunk to the arm, where a small sequencing error separates a scoring strike from a miss. Wearable sensors can capture this movement in the gym, but most deployable systems only classify which punch was thrown rather than assess how well it was thrown. We present Skill Profiling with Attributable Reasoning (SPAR), an eight-IMU garment and pressure-insole system that classifies each punch as expert or novice and treats an explanation of that prediction as feedback. Feedback is only useful if the person receiving it can act on it, so SPAR explains the prediction at three tiers, a per-joint attribution for the analyst, a counterfactual over kinetic-chain layers for the coach, and a plain-language narrative of the two for the athlete. Across 17 participants and 4,713 punches, SPAR reaches a leave-one-participant-out AUC of 0.842 (95% CI [0.769, 0.907] over participants). A frozen time-series foundation model encodes the joint-angle and plantar-force series, and a small transformer trained on the cohort classifies the encoding. We audit the two quantitative tiers and report six themes from a thematic analysis of interviews with six practicing boxing coaches.

items.title: Wearable ECG Quality Assessment: A Deep Learning and Ambulatory Context-Awareness Approach
items.summary: This paper presents and evaluates a Deep Learning-based (DL-based) Signal Quality Assessment (SQA) model to distinguish between clean and noisy ambulatory Electrocardiograms (ECG). The model is trained on Copenhagen Center for Health Technology-Contextualized Arrhythmia Database (CACHET-CADB), which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first ambulatory ECG database with both physical and patient-reported contextual data. The model shows stable performance on different databases such as MIT-databases and the latest PyhsioNet/Cinc Challenge 2021 databases. Subsequently, the paper demonstrates how complicated ECG noise can be investigated by the SQA model and the physical contextual data.

items.title: AnomaSense: Anomaly-based Sensor Activation for Fine-Grained Human Activity Recognition
items.summary: Audio carries rich cues about human activities, and microphones are already built into most wearable devices. However, microphones also capture speech, and this privacy risk limits their use in Human Activity Recognition (HAR). We present AnomaSense, a sensor activation approach for wrist wearables that keeps the microphone off by default and turns it on for at most one second when an unsupervised anomaly detector flags an IMU segment that is likely to produce sound. The captured audio is further masked before it reaches the recognition model. We study 20 activities from 15 participants, organized into five groups in which activities share similar wrist motion but differ in the object or material involved. With IMU data alone, our recognition model reaches 78.98% accuracy in leave-one-participant-out validation. With the short, masked audio windows added, accuracy reaches 96.89% with no masking and stays above 86% when 90% of each one-second audio window is removed. On the same data, the anomaly detector triggers the microphone with 86.46% precision and 74.28% recall relative to sound events. We also report a small preliminary check of automatic speech recognition on masked speech, which shows that contiguous masking degrades recognition far more than point-wise masking at the same masking ratio. Our evaluation is a controlled, offline feasibility study. We describe the threat model, what the approach does and does not protect, and the steps needed before deployment.

items.title: Detecting Agitation Before Behavioral Escalation in Autistic Youth Through Multimodal Wearable Sensing
items.summary: Challenging behaviors including aggression, self-injury, and property destruction are observed in 68% of autistic youth and pose risks to youth and caregivers. These episodes are preceded by agitation, a rising state of distress expressed through movement, vocalization, and autonomic arousal. Its signs are subtle and individualized, and its autonomic components are invisible without instrumentation. We collected upper-body movement from inertial measurement units, physiology from a wrist-worn device, and vocalizations from lapel microphones across 30 clinician-led sessions with 15 autistic youth, paired with expert behavioral annotations. We adapt four pretrained foundation models, one per modality, project each to a shared 128-dimensional space, and fuse them into a single group model. The model detected agitation with an area under the ROC curve of 0.724 at the clinician-annotated onset (within-participant permutation p=0.0005), declining to 0.608 at 30,s before onset. Thirteen of fifteen participants were above chance. A from-scratch configuration reached only 0.58, while frozen and fine-tuned features performed comparably (0.71 and 0.72). Audio contributed most of the signal, and a watch-only configuration stayed near chance. Individualized agitation is therefore detectable, including in unannotated windows preceding the annotated onset, using foundation-model transfer with one shared model rather than one per child.

academic.title: Pre-Deployment Cardiovascular Risk Assessment and Outcomes among United States Antarctic Program Participants: Insights from Contemporary Risk Models
academic.summary: Background: Cardiovascular (CV) screening is critical for personnel deploying to Antarctica, where geographic isolation and limited medical care make the management of acute cardiovascular events challenging. The utility of contemporary risk prediction tools such as the AHA PREVENT equations in this unique population remains uncertain. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 154 individuals referred for enhanced CV evaluation before deployment to the U.S. Antarctic Program (USAP). Participants were evaluated across three temporal cohorts (2018-2020, 2021-2023, and 2024-2026). Demographics, CV risk factors, cardiac testing, and deployment clearance outcomes were collected. Risk was estimated using the Framingham Risk Score (FRS), AHA/ACC Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE), and AHA PREVENT risk models. Results: The cohort was predominantly male (79.9%; mean age 44.6 {+/-} 14.6 years), and abnormal ECG was the most common referral trigger (70.8%). Median 10-year risk was low by PREVENT and FRS and borderline elevated by PCE (PREVENT 2.7% [IQR 1.1-6.6], FRS 2.3% [IQR 0.5-7.1], and PCE 6.1% [IQR 2.4-9.2]). Among 72 participants with all scores, 51% were classified discordantly; PREVENT ASCVD agreed closely with FRS (=0.77) but poorly with PCE (=0.24-0.35), which consistently estimated higher risk. PCE was calculable in 52.6% versus 70.8% for PREVENT. Overall, 132 participants (85.7%) were cleared for deployment, while 8 (5.2%) were not physically qualified (NPQ); 6 of these NPQs were due to cardiovascular causes. Of 22 cardiac medical evacuations during the study period, 21 involved individuals without prior advanced cardiovascular screening. One screened individual was evacuated for symptoms subsequently found to have no cardiac cause. Conclusions: Risk calculators disagree substantially in the fitness-selected population. academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6534: Detection and Classification of Physiological Activation States Through Biosignal Analysis Using Machine Learning
academic.summary: Monitoring autonomic nervous system responses offers significant potential for personalized health applications and early intervention. This study presents a machine learning framework for binary classification of physiological activation states using electrocardiogram (ECG) and respiratory (RESP) signals from the WESAD dataset. Stress and amusement were grouped as Activation, whereas baseline and meditation were grouped as Non-Activation. The processing pipeline incorporates R-peak detection, temporal segmentation, handcrafted feature extraction, and subject-independent evaluation. Conventional machine learning classifiers and deep learning architectures were evaluated, together with a proposed Hybrid Multi-Scale Temporal Convolutional-Conformer (MST-Conformer) combining temporal representations learned from ECG and RESP waveforms with handcrafted physiological features. Performance was assessed using 15-fold Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validation. Adding respiration-derived features to ECG-derived features improved conventional machine learning performance, increasing the highest balanced accuracy from 0.752 to 0.807 and AUC from 0.802 to 0.886. The complete Hybrid MST-Conformer incorporating 27 physiological features achieved a mean accuracy of 0.825, balanced accuracy of 0.820, F1-score of 0.763, and AUC of 0.904. Subject-level analysis also revealed substantial physiological heterogeneity. These results support the potential of combining learned temporal representations with handcrafted physiological information for subject-independent physiological activation classification.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 6511: Development of a Wearable Torsion Sensor Utilizing a Geometric Model and a Hysteresis-Compensated Calibration Engine
academic.summary: Measuring torsional movement is crucial for tracking human kinematics in applications such as virtual reality, biomechanics, rehabilitation, and soft robotic joints. However, continuous, non-invasive torsion measurement remains challenging due to multi-axial deformations, where existing methods rely heavily on empirical data fitting or computationally expensive deep learning models requiring vast training datasets. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a training-free, highly precise torsion estimation framework that converts soft resistive strain sensor data into forearm rotation angles using closed-form kinematic-geometric modeling. Two geometric representations-the Cylinder Model and Truncated Cone Model-are established to analytically map non-linear tensile strain to torsion angles. Additionally, an online calibration algorithm is integrated to mitigate cumulative measurement drift caused by viscoelastic hysteresis. Under static conditions, the proposed models achieved a high coefficient of determination (R2 = 0.9888) against reference IMU data. In dynamic trials, the hysteresis compensation algorithm maintained robust tracking performance (R2 = 0.8033), achieving an angular root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 4.12° and a cycle peak prominence relative error of 0.42% for the Truncated Cone Model. In this single-subject proof-of-concept feasibility study (n = 1), the proposed framework demonstrated the feasibility of continuous torsional motion tracking through a training-free geometric approach, providing a preliminary foundation for future evaluation in wearable systems and soft robotics.

academic.title: GlucoSense: early diabetes risk assessment via fusion of human activity recognition and glucose prediction
academic.summary: Non-Insulin-Dependent Diabetes Mellitus (NIDDM) is a chronic and progressive metabolic disease characterized by chronically high blood glucose levels. It is a disease with an often asymptomatic onset, which means that a high percentage of affected individuals remain unidentified until quite far in the disease process, thereby underlining the importance of a good, reliable screening instrument for proactive detection. In this paper, GlucoSense is introduced as a single framework for early NIDDM risk stratification by combining Human Activity Recognition (HAR) with continuous blood glucose forecasting using two Graph Attention Network version 2 (GATv2)-based architectures. The first is a HAR module trained with smartphone triaxial accelerometer data that covers 23 activity classes, while the second is a glucose prediction module trained with the OhioT1DM dataset to predict glucose levels for a 30 min horizon. Unlike sequential models, GlucoSense encodes complex dependencies between movement patterns, cardiac activity, nutrition, and glycemic behaviour by modeling relationships in a graph structure. The study was longitudinal, spanning 90 days, with six participants. Three important clinical parameters, mean glucose level, time above hyperglycemic level, and glycemic coefficient of variance were calculated. The system was able to correctly identify metabolically healthy individuals and those with prediabetic patterns. The framework was cross-validated with HbA1c laboratory tests to verify the clinical consistency of the framework. Both modules were benchmarked against sequential, convolutional, attention-based, and graph-based baselines under an identical protocol with five independent runs. The glucose module lowered the root mean squared error from 31.82 mg/dL for an LSTM baseline to 25.60 mg/dL, and the activity module reached 98.50% accuracy, with every difference confirmed by paired significance testing and reported with 95% confidence intervals. academic.title: Contactless gait-derived features as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity in adolescents
academic.summary: Timely assessment of depression severity in adolescents is essential for guiding clinical care, yet conventional evaluations rely on episodic clinical assessments and symptom rating scales. Contactless gait analysis offers a potentially scalable approach to capturing objective behavioral features associated with depression. Here, we introduce the Long-Distance 3D Adolescent Depression Gait Dataset (LD3D-ADG), comprising depth-sensor gait recordings from 119 adolescents at a single center, including 39 healthy controls, 41 with mild depression, and 39 with moderate-to-severe depression. We developed UMLPA-GCN, a graph convolutional network that models spatiotemporal gait dynamics across three anatomically defined skeletal partitions. In participant-independent five-fold cross-validation, UMLPA-GCN achieved 75.63% classification accuracy, a macro-F1 score of 75.52%, and a macro-area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.839 (95% confidence interval, 0.779--0.899). Class-specific recall was 87.18%, 63.41%, and 76.92% for healthy controls, mild depression, and moderate-to-severe depression, respectively. At the participant level, reduced arm swing, slower pelvic movement, restricted joint range of motion, and greater arm-swing asymmetry were identified as leading potential digital biomarkers contributing to depression severity assessment, associated with higher 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence for contactless digital depression severity stratification in adolescents. Further external and prospective validation is needed to establish their utility for longitudinal monitoring and timely clinical assessment.

academic.title: Task-evoked eye movements as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults
academic.summary: Objective digital measures of depression severity could complement conventional symptom assessments and facilitate more timely clinical evaluation. Here, we investigated whether task-evoked eye movements provide interpretable behavioral markers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults. In this single-center, cross-sectional study, 155 participants aged 14--20 years completed emotional-spatial free-viewing and memory-guided recall tasks and were stratified by 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. We examined 19 prespecified eye-movement features across six task-informed domains using covariate-adjusted ordinal-trend models. Greater depression severity was associated with lower gaze-allocation entropy (standardized $β=-0.599$), fewer inter-area switches ($β=-0.526$), longer first target-entry latency ($β=0.572$), and lower target dwell proportion ($β=-0.678$; all false-discovery-rate-adjusted $q<0.001$). Emotion-specific attentional-bias measures were not associated with severity, whereas associations involving fixation dispersion weakened after adjustment for anxiety symptoms. In a complementary machine-learning analysis incorporating 44 candidate eye-movement features and demographic covariates, a three-stage cascade classifier achieved the highest four-class stratification performance (accuracy, 0.665; macro-F1, 0.670; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.869), outperforming single-stage and two-stage approaches. Together, these findings identify altered visual exploration and memory-guided gaze control as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity, rather than generalized negative attentional bias. These results support further prospective evaluation of task-evoked eye tracking as a complementary approach for timely severity assessment and clinical decision support.

academic.title: FALLNEST: Dual-Domain Dataset Condensation of Imbalanced IMU Data for Wearable Fall Detection
academic.summary: Wearable fall detection is hampered by rare fall events, scarce labeled IMU data, and the cost of training deep models on large, imbalanced corpora. Existing methods either rely on hand-crafted features with shallow classifiers, which limits learning from raw signals, or train deep networks on full datasets that require re-sampling to counter class skew and demand substantial data and compute. To address this, we propose a novel Fall detection framework via Normalized-gradient and Embedding matched Synthetic Time-frequency condensation, dubbed FALLNEST, a data-centric approach that distills large, imbalanced IMU datasets into tiny, class-balanced synthetic training sets. Building on dual-domain time-series condensation (CondTSC), FALLNEST introduces a fall-specific 7-channel input with accelerometer vector magnitude, class-balanced K-Means initialization, and normalized gradient matching with gradient clipping, combined with MMD-based embedding alignment and multi-view Fourier-domain augmentation, so that class balance arises from the condensed set itself rather than from re-sampling. We evaluate on SisFall, KFall, and MobiFall using strict subject-wise splits and naturally imbalanced test sets, reporting accuracy, Macro-F1, and PR-AUC over five seeds. A 102K-parameter TinyCNN trained on only 32 to 146 synthetic windows (about only 1% of the training windows) reaches 93.5-95.8% mean accuracy and 0.89-0.98 PR-AUC, with standard deviations of 1.0-1.7% in accuracy, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach.

academic.title: ECG-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Targeted Electrocardiogram Waveform Evolution
academic.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need supervision that targets evolving weaknesses and remains faithful to waveform evidence. We introduce ECG-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework combining verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search. Signal remeasurement verifies waveform edits; construction errors guide generator repair, while learner errors motivate interventions compared on a separate selection set. Across seven benchmarks, three rounds raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean question-answering accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04% and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. Across the retained trajectory, the preferred supervision shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts. Continued feedback correction yields diminishing external gains. These results motivate separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and checking whether gains on the feedback set transfer to independent benchmarks.

academic.title: A Co-Located MMG-FES Wearable Interface for Action-Updated State-Gated Stimulation
academic.summary: Functional electrical stimulation (FES) assists movement, but fixed schedules cannot track how a repeatedly activated muscle changes, and surface electromyography (EMG) near the stimulation electrodes is often obscured by artifacts. Prior work recorded mechanomyography (MMG) passively during closed-loop FES cycling and estimated FES-induced fatigue or predicted fatigue for FES control, without gating stimulation with stimulated-site MMG. In this study, we present VG-FES, a wearable module co-locating microphone-based MMG, programmable charge-balanced biphasic stimulation, and embedded state-gated control at one on-skin thigh site. After each action, we compare rectus femoris (RF) mean power frequency (MPF) with an early-session baseline of the same direction, giving a relative state. A threshold on its window means enables fixed-duration bursts separated by rest periods. During onboard stimulation, MMG remained recordable, whereas near-site EMG was artifact-dominated. Under prolonged external stimulation, cycle-wise MMG tracked an independent local-pressure reference (Spearman rho = 0.968). In leave-one-session-out evaluation on 2284 squat actions (11 sessions, eight participants), MMG-based action segmentation reached an event-detection F1 of 0.923 and direction classification a balanced accuracy of 0.925. Online, over 15.69 min of self-paced squats, one participant received four bursts while MMG acquisition and action monitoring continued. Mechanical feedback from the stimulated site offers wearable FES and assistive robotics a per-action basis for state-gated stimulation.

academic.title: Integration of Ecological Momentary Assessment and Intervention With Wearable-Based Digital Phenotypes to Treat Anxiety in Young Adults: Mixed Methods Experimental Study

academic.title: AI-Driven Urge Regulation Assistant (AURA): Designing Preemptive Smart Wearables for Smoking Cessation
academic.summary: Smoking cessation remains a complex self-regulatory challenge, often undermined by cue-triggered cravings arising from habitual, emotional, and social contexts. Existing wearable cessation systems are largely reactive, detecting smoking events only after lapses occur and thus missing the critical window for timely intervention. Guided by cue-reactivity theory and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), we argue that future digital health systems should shift from retrospective feedback toward proactive craving management that supports user autonomy and competence. To inform the design of such systems, we present a formative pilot qualitative study involving semi-structured interviews with 10 smokers and ex-smokers from a multi-ethnic Asian population, a demographic underrepresented in current wearable AI and smoking cessation research. Through an iterative co-design interview process, we examine (1) the barriers and facilitators to smoking cessation and (2) the desired design features of wearable systems targeting cravings before lapses occur. Our findings identify key craving predictors across habitual, emotional, and social dimensions, alongside user-preferred intervention strategies such as social accountability, personalized support, rewards, and just-in-time distraction techniques. Participants also emphasized the importance of trust, privacy, personalization, and non-judgmental interaction styles. These insights directly inform the design of AURA, a novel smartwatch-smartphone ecosystem for proactive craving detection and intervention using commercially available wearable devices.

academic.title: BeatFlow-ECG: Rectified Flow for ECG Reconstruction from Indirect Wearable Signals
academic.summary: Continuous cardiac monitoring outside clinical settings requires signals that are both informative and practical to collect during daily life. Electrocardiography (ECG) provides rich information about cardiac rhythm and waveform morphology, while wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) is easier to acquire continuously but is only an indirect cardiovascular measurement and is highly sensitive to motion. We present BeatFlow-ECG, a conditional rectified-flow model for reconstructing single-channel ECG from synchronized PPG and inertial measurements. BeatFlow-ECG models reconstruction as conditional transport from noise to ECG using a convolutional encoder-decoder with a transformer bottleneck and explicit flow-time conditioning. Motion information is incorporated through IMU-derived conditioning features, motion-dependent loss weighting, and an easy-to-hard training curriculum. We evaluate the model under leave-one-subject-out protocols on PPG-DaLiA and WESAD. BeatFlow-ECG achieves the best results among the evaluated deterministic, adversarial, and diffusion-based baselines across all reported waveform and beat-timing metrics, with Pearson correlations of 0.983 and 0.986 and R-peak F1 scores of 0.946 and 0.955, respectively. Compared with Conditional DDPM-1D, L1 error decreases from 0.085 to 0.062 on PPG-DaLiA and from 0.074 to 0.055 on WESAD. Additional analyses on PPG-DaLiA show higher correlation in fixed R-peak-relative waveform regions and lower reconstruction error across low-, medium-, and high-motion subsets.

academic.title: REFIT: Recognize, Fix, and Test Wearable Sensor Placement Shifts without Labels
academic.summary: We present REFIT, an input calibration for frozen activity-recognition models whose inertial sensors are worn differently at deployment than in training. When users move a watch to the other wrist or put a strap sensor back on turned, the model sees the same motion on changed axes. REFIT undoes such shifts without labels or retraining. It describes them by families of axis transforms, such as reflections and rotations, and fits each family to the user's data so that simple statistics match those of the training data. The family that removes most of the mismatch names the shift. REFIT fixes the shift by applying the best member of that family before the frozen model and re-estimating its normalization statistics. It tests the fixed model with a label-free accuracy estimate and asks the user to re-wear the sensor when it is low. Experiments on real left/right sensor pairs and on real and simulated re-attachment show that REFIT outperforms label-free test-time adaptation methods on every dataset and restores most of the accuracy lost to re-attachment. It names injected shifts far more reliably than a confidence-based selector. After a correction over all signed permutations of the axes, the estimate separates successful from failed corrections.

academic.title: Label-Efficient Deep Learning for ECG Delineation: A Multi-Dataset Benchmark against Widely Used Delineation Tools
academic.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) delineation, the identification of waveform boundaries, is a foundational step that translates raw ECG signals into clinically interpretable measurements. Deep learning has advanced this task but remains dependent on costly expert annotations. Label-efficient strategies such as self-supervised pretraining and semi-supervised learning are expected to ease this burden, yet it remains unclear whether they yield reliable delineation and whether the deep models they produce outperform the delineation tools used in practice. We address this in two stages. First, comparing self-supervised objectives with supervised or semi-supervised fine-tuning across one internal and four external datasets, we find that pretraining helps but the objective matters, and that the value of semi-supervised fine-tuning depends on the pretraining objective. Second, we benchmark the selected deep learning model against widely used open-source (NeuroKit2, Prominence, ECGdeli) and commercial (CalECG) tools using three complementary metrics. The model ranks best on every metric and dataset, outperforming the strongest tool by a clear margin on the rhythm-diverse set (mIoU 71.3 vs. 54.8%; averaged point-wise sensitivity 92.6 vs. 76.4%), and degrades the least from sinus to arrhythmia. A rhythm-stratified and point-wise analysis further characterizes the distinctive behavior of each tool, yielding practical guidance for tool selection. These results provide systematic, multi-dataset evidence that self-supervised pretraining is effective for ECG delineation and enables a label-efficiently trained deep learning model to outperform widely used delineation tools by leveraging abundant unlabeled data. This supports adopting such models in diverse, real-world clinical settings.

academic.title: Characterizing the Performance Gap in Human Activity Recognition for Older Adults
academic.summary: Human activity recognition (HAR) from wrist-worn accelerometers is increasingly used for health and behavioral tracking. Yet, most wearable HAR models are developed and evaluated on datasets dominated by younger adults, leaving it unclear whether benchmark progress generalizes across age groups. In this work, we leverage MyMove, our carefully annotated, free-living older-adult HAR dataset (mean age 71), to evaluate deep-learning architectures and training regimes under both leave-one-subject-out and cross-dataset transfer. We find that improvements on younger-adult benchmarks fail to transfer equally to data collected from older adults, resulting in a persistent and often widening performance gap. However, richer representations, particularly frozen self-supervised features pretrained on the age-diverse UK Biobank dataset, substantially improve performance on data from older adults and consistently narrow the performance gap, at modest cost to younger-adult performance, though disparities remain. These findings suggest that benchmark gains and architectural scaling alone provide an incomplete picture of progress in wearable HAR, and broader advances may require representations that better capture population diversity, alongside personalized adaptation to individual movement patterns and routines.

academic.title: Open-Source Multi-Wire SPI Readout for Wearable Ultrasound Probes
academic.summary: Wearable ultrasound probes must transfer increasingly large acquisition payloads while maintaining compact, low-power electronics. In TinyProbe, the current bottleneck in data transfer occurs between the acquisition FPGA and the wireless system controller. This work presents an open-source, multi-wire SPI readout interface that uses serial command and address phases followed by a build-time-selectable dual- or quad-lane payload phase that is intended to address this bottleneck by increasing the potential bandwidth over the wifi limit while retaining compatibility with the Microcontroller-centric wearable US architecture. The interface emulates a serial flash memory, enabling compatibility with a broad range of microcontroller families and their existing peripheral interfaces. On the FPGA, the data path connects the existing acquisition FIFOs to the SPI interface through clock-domain crossing, sample reshaping, and packing into 32-bit words. Dual-SPI readout is integrated into the existing IGLOO2/SiWG917 TinyProbe architecture and verified at an SCLK frequency of 5 MHz. A separate Kria K26 testbed is used to characterize the FPGA SPI interface independently of the acquisition and wireless subsystems, demonstrating error-free transfers at SCLK frequencies up to 66 MHz. These measurements identify the SiWG917 multi-lane SPI implementation as the next bandwidth-limiting component and motivate a future upgrade of the system controller. The HDL and MCU implementations are released under a permissive open-source license.

academic.title: Noninvasive Interstitial Glucose Estimation Using Wearables and Machine Learning in Healthy Individuals and Individuals With Obesity: Observational Cohort Study
academic.summary: Background: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) can facilitate weight management and lower the risk of metabolic diseases by providing real-time feedback on glycemic responses, thereby enabling more informed lifestyle decisions. However, current CGM systems remain constrained by invasiveness, cost, and short sensor lifespan, limiting their practicality for guiding individualized postprandial low-glycemic diets. Objective: Extending earlier proof-of-concept findings, this study aimed to validate an interstitial glucose (IG) machine learning algorithm in real-world environments using multimodal, continuous data collected from wearable sensors and smartwatches. In the long term, we aim to embed a noninvasive, sensor-based algorithm for estimating tissue glucose within mobile health apps and postprandial low-glycemic diet frameworks to enable scalable, personalized prevention strategies. Methods: We conducted a 2-week study phase during which participants continuously wore 2 noninvasive sensor devices: a scientific sensor wristband (Empatica EmbracePlus) and a commercially available smartwatch (Fitbit Sense 2). As a reference measurement, an invasive CGM sensor (Abbott FreeStyle Libre 3) measured IG levels. For metabolic characterization, 1-point fasting blood and urine samples were collected, and deep phenotyping using state-of-the-art nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and bioelectrical impedance analysis was performed. For participants with overweight and obesity, clinical standard parameters focusing on glucose metabolism were analyzed. Results: A total of 74 participants, 34 (46%) healthy controls and 40 (54%) metabolically at-risk (MR) individuals, simultaneously used an invasive CGM device together with 2 noninvasive wristbands over 2 weeks. Healthy controls were characterized by a mean age of 24.53 (SD 3.68) years and a mean BMI of 22.36 (SD 2.16) kg/m². In contrast, the MR cohort had a mean age of 55.38 (SD 15.08) years and a mean BMI of 35.38 (SD 4.91) kg

academic.title: ECG-Scroll: A Long-Horizon, Streaming Benchmark and Agent Environment for Interpretation of Ambulatory Electrocardiograms
academic.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can now interpret a standard ten-second, twelve-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) with clinically grounded, reward-verified reasoning. Real cardiac monitoring is different. Ambulatory (Holter) and telemetry recordings span hours to days and are read as they stream in, and their clinically decisive findings are paroxysmal, brief episodes buried in an otherwise unremarkable trace. Such a recording cannot be held in one context at diagnostic resolution, and its future has not yet happened, so a reader must work online, deciding what to measure now, committing evidence to memory as it passes, and reporting events as they occur. We recast long-duration ECG interpretation as a long-horizon, online (streaming, causal) sequential decision process and introduce ECG-Scroll. As a benchmark, long ambulatory recordings are streamed to an agent chunk by chunk, and it must localize, quantify, and promptly flag paroxysmal events without access to future signal; because the underlying signal is retained, every answer is checkable against objective ground truth, giving rule-based rather than judge-based rewards, and the streaming formulation adds a metric batch evaluation cannot express, the detection latency between an event's onset and the moment the agent records it. As an agent environment, it is a fixed, gym-style interaction layer that exercises three competencies single-glance ECG models never touch: Memory, Tool use through signal-grounded measurement rather than reading pixels, and Planning of what to measure now and when to commit. We release 390 whole-recording instances spanning 2,536 hours of two-lead ambulatory ECG and evaluate a signal-threshold rule agent alongside off-the-shelf LLM agents online, characterizing how they use memory, tools, and planning and where the benchmark's head-room lies.

academic.title: Skill Profiling with Attributable Reasoning (SPAR): A Wearable Analysis System for Boxing
academic.summary: A punch is a ballistic, full-body action driven by a kinetic chain running from the legs through the trunk to the arm, where a small sequencing error separates a scoring strike from a miss. Wearable sensors can capture this movement in the gym, but most deployable systems only classify which punch was thrown rather than assess how well it was thrown. We present Skill Profiling with Attributable Reasoning (SPAR), an eight-IMU garment and pressure-insole system that classifies each punch as expert or novice and treats an explanation of that prediction as feedback. Feedback is only useful if the person receiving it can act on it, so SPAR explains the prediction at three tiers, a per-joint attribution for the analyst, a counterfactual over kinetic-chain layers for the coach, and a plain-language narrative of the two for the athlete. Across 17 participants and 4,713 punches, SPAR reaches a leave-one-participant-out AUC of 0.842 (95% CI [0.769, 0.907] over participants). A frozen time-series foundation model encodes the joint-angle and plantar-force series, and a small transformer trained on the cohort classifies the encoding. We audit the two quantitative tiers and report six themes from a thematic analysis of interviews with six practicing boxing coaches.

academic.title: Wearable ECG Quality Assessment: A Deep Learning and Ambulatory Context-Awareness Approach
academic.summary: This paper presents and evaluates a Deep Learning-based (DL-based) Signal Quality Assessment (SQA) model to distinguish between clean and noisy ambulatory Electrocardiograms (ECG). The model is trained on Copenhagen Center for Health Technology-Contextualized Arrhythmia Database (CACHET-CADB), which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first ambulatory ECG database with both physical and patient-reported contextual data. The model shows stable performance on different databases such as MIT-databases and the latest PyhsioNet/Cinc Challenge 2021 databases. Subsequently, the paper demonstrates how complicated ECG noise can be investigated by the SQA model and the physical contextual data.

academic.title: AnomaSense: Anomaly-based Sensor Activation for Fine-Grained Human Activity Recognition
academic.summary: Audio carries rich cues about human activities, and microphones are already built into most wearable devices. However, microphones also capture speech, and this privacy risk limits their use in Human Activity Recognition (HAR). We present AnomaSense, a sensor activation approach for wrist wearables that keeps the microphone off by default and turns it on for at most one second when an unsupervised anomaly detector flags an IMU segment that is likely to produce sound. The captured audio is further masked before it reaches the recognition model. We study 20 activities from 15 participants, organized into five groups in which activities share similar wrist motion but differ in the object or material involved. With IMU data alone, our recognition model reaches 78.98% accuracy in leave-one-participant-out validation. With the short, masked audio windows added, accuracy reaches 96.89% with no masking and stays above 86% when 90% of each one-second audio window is removed. On the same data, the anomaly detector triggers the microphone with 86.46% precision and 74.28% recall relative to sound events. We also report a small preliminary check of automatic speech recognition on masked speech, which shows that contiguous masking degrades recognition far more than point-wise masking at the same masking ratio. Our evaluation is a controlled, offline feasibility study. We describe the threat model, what the approach does and does not protect, and the steps needed before deployment.

academic.title: Detecting Agitation Before Behavioral Escalation in Autistic Youth Through Multimodal Wearable Sensing
academic.summary: Challenging behaviors including aggression, self-injury, and property destruction are observed in 68% of autistic youth and pose risks to youth and caregivers. These episodes are preceded by agitation, a rising state of distress expressed through movement, vocalization, and autonomic arousal. Its signs are subtle and individualized, and its autonomic components are invisible without instrumentation. We collected upper-body movement from inertial measurement units, physiology from a wrist-worn device, and vocalizations from lapel microphones across 30 clinician-led sessions with 15 autistic youth, paired with expert behavioral annotations. We adapt four pretrained foundation models, one per modality, project each to a shared 128-dimensional space, and fuse them into a single group model. The model detected agitation with an area under the ROC curve of 0.724 at the clinician-annotated onset (within-participant permutation p=0.0005), declining to 0.608 at 30,s before onset. Thirteen of fifteen participants were above chance. A from-scratch configuration reached only 0.58, while frozen and fine-tuned features performed comparably (0.71 and 0.72). Audio contributed most of the signal, and a watch-only configuration stayed near chance. Individualized agitation is therefore detectable, including in unannotated windows preceding the annotated onset, using foundation-model transfer with one shared model rather than one per child.

scarcityTaxonomy.note: Top Signals selection rubric. Each Top Signals item MUST be labeled with exactly one category from `categories`, assigned a frequency anchor (`annual`/`quarterly`/`monthly`), and scored as `base_score × anchor_weight`. LLM only does category+anchor matching — it does NOT need historical knowledge (categories define scarcity, not LLM memory). Revise quarterly based on dogfooding.

anchor_definitions.annual: Once-a-year or rarer event within this category (e.g., FDA's first consumer-grade AFib clearance for a wearable — happens at most once a year globally).
anchor_definitions.quarterly: Few-per-year event within this category (e.g., a major vendor's new regulatory clearance in a new jurisdiction).
anchor_definitions.monthly: Routine-but-still-notable within this category (e.g., another vendor achieving a similar clearance that's already established).

categories.criteria: FDA 510(k) / De Novo / PMA, CE mark MDR, NMPA certification, PMDA, TGA — for a wearable health feature. Peer-reviewed multi-site prospective clinical validation also qualifies.
examples_positive: Apple Watch gets FDA clearance for new sleep apnea detection
Samsung Health Monitor BP approved in US
Oura ring NMPA class-II certification
examples_negative: Another vendor clones an already-approved feature in a new region (→ monthly anchor, not annual)

categories.criteria: Company or academic publicly releases model weights, pretrained foundation model, large labeled dataset, or production-grade SDK/code for wearable/physiological signals. Must be usable (not just a paper claiming 'code coming soon').
examples_positive: Meta releases wearable foundation model weights on HuggingFace
Stanford/Apple release 1M-ECG labeled dataset
Google open-sources Fitbit sleep staging model
examples_negative: Academic paper promises code release but repo is empty

categories.criteria: M&A, major exec/founder departure or appointment at a wearable company, large funding round (≥$50M), strategic pivot announcement. Affects competitive landscape or talent flow.
examples_positive: Google acquires Oura
Shwetak Patel leaves Google Health for X startup
WHOOP pivots from consumer to B2B-clinical

categories.criteria: Consumer wearable first-time integration of a physical/biochemical sensing modality (non-invasive BP, non-invasive glucose, EMG, sweat cortisol, SpHb, real-time hydration, etc.). Must ship in a real product, not just a research paper.
examples_positive: Samsung ships first consumer non-invasive glucose on Galaxy Watch
Apple adds wrist-based cuffless BP to Series X
Oura integrates continuous sweat-lactate sensor
examples_negative: New optical HR sensor iteration in existing form factor (already-done modality)
Academic prototype for a new sensor — belongs in algorithmic_breakthrough or open_release if qualifying

categories.criteria: New SOTA with concrete metric on wearable/physiological task, OR foundation-model / self-supervised training at ≥10M-sample scale, OR on-device breakthrough with specific latency/size/power numbers. Must have reproducible evidence (paper with code, benchmark result).
examples_positive: ECG foundation model at 11M samples with systematic SSL comparison (example)
On-device AFib detection at <5ms/inference on Apple S10 chip
New sleep-stage SOTA on SHHS with 3pp gain
examples_negative: Incremental +1pp gain with cherry-picked test set

categories.criteria: Prospective or multi-site clinical study with n≥10,000 participants OR multi-center design, wearable-derived endpoint, peer-reviewed or at top conference.
examples_positive: Ultrahuman Ring N=3086 longitudinal sleep study (today's example — note: n<10k but near-threshold + longitudinal design keeps it in this category at monthly anchor)
All of Us cohort wearable analysis n>50k
Apple Heart Study n=419k

categories.criteria: Wearable vendor first-time entry into new go-to-market category: clinical services, B2B/B2B2C, insurance, subscription, EHR integration, pharma partnership. Must be a real product launch, not a trial balloon.
examples_positive: WHOOP launches clinician video visits + HealthEx EHR integration (today's example)
Oura partners with large insurer for reimbursed rings
Apple Watch Atrial Fibrillation History gets CMS reimbursement code
examples_negative: New subscription tier of existing product

categories.criteria: HealthKit / Health Connect / Samsung Health SDK / Huawei Health Kit / Wear OS schema, new data type, permission, or interoperability standard (FHIR wearables profile). Must be shipping, not WWDC keynote hype.
examples_positive: HealthKit adds glucose trend data type in watchOS 27
Health Connect adds cross-app mental-health schema
New IEEE standard for wearable data exchange ratified
